newsitem.title: USA: U.S. revises down January, February trade gaps.
newsitem.headline: U.S. revises down January, February trade gaps.

text.p: The U.S. performance on trade was slightly less woeful in January and February than previously thought, corrected Commerce Department figures issued Friday showed.

Revised figures incorporating corrections to the government's previous estimates of imported oil had the effect of pushing down the cumulative two-month deficit on total goods and services trade this year by $1.5 billion from the comparable first two months of 1996.

The Commerce Department said the U.S. trade deficit in January was a still-hefty $12.33 billion instead of $12.67 billion while the February gap between exports and imports was $10.42 billion instead of $11.56 billion.

The department initially reported the higher February deficit number on April 17, saying the monthly deficit had narrowed just 8.5 percent to $11.56 billion. But after the revision to January, the February deficit actually fell by a much sharper 15.5 percent.

The Commerce Department had corrected its February trade estimate hours after its initial report on April 17, saying "data reporting errors" had incorrectly assigned $1.1 billion of crude petroleum imports to February. In fact, the oil entered the country at an earlier time.

Analysts said they could not recall such a dramatic correction in a government economic indicator. Financial markets closely track the monthly trade and other indicators, which are collected, compiled and released under strict security, for signs of the economy's performance.

Since billions of dollars are regularly added or subtracted to stock and bond prices within minutes of the release of official indicators, analysts said the accuracy of the government-compiled statistics was critical.

The Commerce Department conducted a detailed examination of its crude petroleum import data after questions arose about its first estimate of the February trade deficit, ultimately shifting some blame to the Treasury Department's Customs Bureau.

It said the examination "revealed that some of the documents submitted for February were actually related to crude petroleum import transactions occurring in 1996 and 1995" and said it uses import and export documents passed on to it by Customs.

The revised trade figures show that the volume of February crude oil imports averaged 7.36 million barrels a day instead of 9.33 million and that January imports were running at 6.99 million barrels daily rather than 7.5 million.
The correct value of the imported petroleum in February was $4.22 billion, not $5.28 billion, and in January it was $4.77 billion instead of $5.11 billion, the Commerce Department said.
